articles.title: AI can widen science — but only if institutions stop rewarding the already measurable
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02961-zFunders, journals and universities must reward the creation of new scientific terrain, not just the efficient mining of old ground.
articles.content:
The use of artificial intelligence in science is producing a conundrum: individual researchers are becoming more productive, while the scientific enterprise as a whole is exploring a narrower range of ideas.

Will AI spark a scientific renaissance — or a diffuse monoculture?

For instance, academics who adopt AI tools publish about three times as many papers and receive nearly five times as many citations as do their peers. Yet, analyses of the scientific literature show that AI-assisted research spans 4.6% less topical ground than does non-AI work, with this pattern being present in more than 70% of the subfields studied1.

The problem is not technological, but institutional. AI tools expand scientists’ capacity to explore, but systemic incentives mean that researchers use this capability to focus more intensely on problems that institutions can easily recognize, evaluate and reward, rather than breaking new ground.

These dynamics did not originate with AI: research has shown that papers and patents have become less disruptive over the past six decades2. But AI is accelerating these changes, because speed and pattern recognition in large bodies of work are precisely what a narrowing system will focus on most intensively. The academic career structure reinforces this effect. AI makes extending a familiar research line faster and cheaper than entering unfamiliar terrain, and existing incentive systems reward such speed.

To address these concerns, we put forward three recommendations.

Make new terrain measurable

Current funding systems overwhelmingly reward the downstream exploitation of existing data rather than the upstream creation of new data sets and measurement capabilities. By applying increasingly powerful AI models to public data sets, researchers can often generate publishable results at relatively low cost.

For instance, Google’s Graph Networks for Materials Exploration (GNoME) is a deep-learning tool that has identified 381,000 candidate stable inorganic crystals, expanding the known materials landscape by an order of magnitude3. Meanwhile, AlphaFold, a protein-structure prediction system created by DeepMind in London, has generated more than 214 million potential protein structures, making biological interactions inspectable at an unprecedented scale4.

Artificial-intelligence tool AlphaFold has been used to identify millions of protein structures.Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty

By contrast, building a longitudinal cohort study or launching a biodiversity-monitoring programme can take years of sustained investment before any publishable findings are produced.

This asymmetry is widening: the costs of making predictions with AI models have fallen roughly 100-fold in the past two years, whereas building new observational infrastructure still carries high long-term operational costs5–7. This means that the gap between what is cheap to exploit and what is expensive to explore widens every few months.

We call on funders to deliberately subsidize the data infrastructure, especially in neglected domains such as diseases that have been excluded from major cohort studies. These investments are slow and unglamorous, but they are essential if AI is to work with observations from previously overlooked areas.

Stop punishing pivots

Universities and funding agencies must stop penalizing researchers who use AI to enter new fields. AI tools reduce the informational cost of pivoting — an ecologist entering genomics, for example, can now traverse unfamiliar literature faster. But evaluation systems still penalize pivots into other subfields8. Hiring committees assess candidates on a continuous publication record in a single domain and funding agencies often treat preliminary data from the applicant’s previous work as a prerequisite for support.
articles.reasoning: The article discusses how AI is transforming scientific research productivity and proposes institutional changes to maximize AI's positive impact by encouraging exploration of new scientific areas. This represents a significant and inspiring advancement in science and technology with broad societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: AI boosts scientific productivity but needs new rewards to encourage discovery
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists are using artificial intelligence (AI) more in their research. This helps them work faster and publish more papers. But there is a problem: AI-driven research tends to focus on familiar topics instead of exploring new ideas.

**What happened** – Studies show that researchers who use AI publish three times more papers and get five times more citations than others. However, their work covers about 4.6% less variety in topics. This happens because universities and funding groups reward work on known problems, not new or risky ones. AI speeds up research on familiar topics, making it cheaper and easier to get recognized.

**Impact** – This narrowing focus could limit big scientific discoveries. For example, AI tools like Google’s GNoME and DeepMind’s AlphaFold have helped find many new materials and protein structures. But creating new data or starting long-term studies still takes a lot of time and money, and these efforts are not rewarded enough. Without change, science may miss out on important new areas.

**What's next step** – Experts suggest three main changes: first, funders should support building new data and measurement tools, even if results take a long time; second, universities should stop penalizing researchers who switch to new fields using AI; and third, institutions must value exploring new scientific questions as much as working faster on old ones. These steps can help AI widen the range of scientific discovery.

**One-sentence takeaway** – To make AI a tool for broad scientific discovery, institutions need to reward creating new knowledge, not just faster research on familiar topics.

articles.title: AI finds 3D shape that fills all space with a never-repeating pattern
articles.summary: A 3D shape that can tile 3D space, leaving no gaps and never forming a repeating pattern, has been discovered using an AI model. The researcher behind the findings, who has no academic background in the area, says his work has angered professional mathematicians
articles.content:
A 3D shape that can tile 3D space, leaving no gaps and never forming a repeating pattern, has been discovered using an AI model. The researcher behind the findings, who has no academic background in the area, says his work has angered professional mathematicians

The Chair44 3D monotile Ioannis Tsiokos

In 2023, after decades of searching, mathematicians discovered a shape called “the hat” – so named for its passing resemblance to a fedora – that can tile a 2D surface without gaps and without ever creating a repeating pattern. Now, a researcher has used AI to go one dimension better and discover a 3D shape that can do the same thing.

Simple shapes like squares can tile a 2D surface, but will form repeating patterns. So-called aperiodic tiles achieve the former without the latter – you can scroll in any direction, infinitely, and not find a regularly repeating pattern.

That sounds like a nifty but ultimately useless mathematical curiosity, but since the 2023 publication of the 2D tile, it has been used in scientific papers in fields from engineering to chemistry. Some have explored the likely physical properties of a material with hat-shaped crystals. Others have found that structures built using hat-shaped building blocks could be more resistant to fracturing than those built using famously strong honeycomb-like building blocks.

Advertisement

Now, Ioannis Tsiokos, a software developer with no background in mathematics, has used AI to discover a 3D monotile he calls Chair44. He did so by describing the 2D problem to OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra model and asking it to find a similar result in three dimensions.

“Astra found this, I didn’t find the tile,” says Tsiokos. “I gave Astra the theory, I gave it the laws, I gave it the theorems, the Lean code, the papers, and I said: ‘Here’s the problem.’ It’s kind of cheeky: I’ve been in forums with other mathematicians, and [of] course they’re all angry with me… because I don’t have the background to land this result.”

Tsiokos says he also used AI to write the paper describing the finding, and has published around 40 papers in the same way, with another 20 that he is yet to release. But, as he suggests, not all mathematicians are impressed by the way the discovery has been disseminated.

On Time: The physics that makes the universe tick See Jim Al-Khalili at New Scientist Live 2026 Find out more

Chaim Goodman-Strauss at the University of Arkansas described the paper as “basically a piece of slop”, and says that while the result is valid, the paper does little to clarify or explain it. “Incontrovertibly, there’s a very, very pretty result that emerges here,” he says. Goodman-Strauss has since published a paper clarifying Tsiokos’ work.

Felix Flicker at the University of Bristol in the UK has also published a paper showing that Chair44 can be simplified and retain its aperiodicity.

Craig Kaplan at the University of Waterloo, Canada, was one of the researchers behind the 2D aperiodic tile. He says the new paper has “all the usual deficiencies of AI-generated mathematics” in terms of readability and clarity, but that, despite this, the actual shape appears to be a valid solution.

“It goes without saying that many of us have been contemplating the search for a 3D aperiodic monotile, and I can say that it’s a natural question people ask when I give talks on the hat,” says Kaplan. “But I was always daunted by the simple prospect of visualising the problem or candidate solutions. Even if I had some shape that looked promising, how should I go about understanding large 3D assemblies of that shape? Evidently, a computer doesn’t have to struggle as hard.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough in mathematics and AI-assisted discovery: the finding of a 3D aperiodic monotile shape that can fill space without gaps or repeating patterns. This discovery has broad implications for science and engineering, including material science and structural design, showing tangible potential benefits beyond a niche mathematical curiosity. The use of AI to achieve this breakthrough highlights innovative technology application with meaningful impact, despite some controversy over the dissemination and clarity of the findings.

articles.title: Fossil found on Welsh beach ends 'confusion' over 200-million-year-old fish teeth
articles.summary: Fossilised teeth across Europe had been wrongly identified until the latest find in south Wales.
articles.content:
Researchers from Amgueddfa Cymru - Museum Wales worked with State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart and the University of Bristol, where the fossil had been sent for detailed inspection.

They discovered it belonged to a Saurichthys - a predator fish that lived in shallow tropical seas during the Late Triassic period.

"Many teeth from Saurichthys were once mistaken for those of an amphibian, and that misunderstanding continued well into the 20th Century," said Museum Wales curator Cindy Howells.

"This lovely little jaw caused great confusion when it was first found as it bore no resemblance to any known species," she said.

Quinn said the fossils found in the Bristol Channel had come from storms that had happened 200 million years ago.

"It is remarkable that such a delicate fossil survived," she said.

"Although British Triassic fossils have been studied for over 200 years, this is the first bone from Saurichthys ever found in these rocks."

The discovery led to the publication of a scientific paper, external that compared the fossil with those across Europe.

By comparing the new snout with museum specimens from Britain and Europe, it provided clear evidence that fossils originally thought to be Severnichthys were actually a combination of two separate species.

The name Severnichthys had been used for individual teeth and a few small bones that existed in many museum collections. These were even thought to be from amphibians well into the 20th Century, rather than the fish that experts now know they were.

"These predators lived in a shallow tropical sea filled with small limestone islands," paper co-author Dr David Whiteside said of the two species.

"Saurichthys was probably a fast and agile hunter, while Birgeria was larger and more powerful, likely feeding on a wider variety of prey."

Another co-author, Dr Sam Cooper, said: "These fish have a remarkably complicated history.

"It's amazing that a single fossil, found by Jonathan Bow during a spring tide, has helped clear up nearly 200 years of confusion."

This breakthrough has broad scientific relevance and enriches knowledge of Earth's history.

They identified it as belonging to Saurichthys, a fast predator fish that lived about 200 million years ago during the Late Triassic period.

**Impact** – This discovery cleared up confusion that lasted two centuries. It showed that many fossils once thought to be from one species, called Severnichthys, were actually from two different fish species: Saurichthys and Birgeria. articles.title: Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
articles.summary: Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet.
articles.content:
Most of us think of a day as a fixed 24 hours. In reality, Earth's rotation is not perfectly constant.

The difference is tiny, measured in milliseconds, but physicists can detect it. Over time, some days become slightly shorter or longer depending on subtle changes deep inside the planet.

Earth's Core and Mantle Trade Momentum

For roughly three decades, scientists have known that Earth's liquid core does not always rotate at the same rate. Changes in the planet's magnetic field have revealed that the liquid core can gradually speed up over several decades, then slow down during the following decades.

At the same time, the mantle, the roughly 3,000 kilometer thick rocky layer that includes the crust, responds in the opposite direction. When the core speeds up, the mantle slows slightly. When the core slows, the mantle speeds up.

This exchange happens because Earth's total angular momentum must remain constant.

Even very small changes in the mantle's rotation are enough to alter the length of a day by a few milliseconds.

A Hidden Gravitational Tug Inside Earth

Scientists have long struggled to explain exactly how the core and mantle exchange this rotational momentum.

In a new study published Sept. 23 in Nature, University of Alberta physics PhD student Huifeng Zhang and professor Mathieu Dumberry present a possible answer.

Their work shows that small changes in the rotational speed of Earth's inner core, the solid region at the planet's center, can create what scientists call a "gravitational torque." Because the inner core is not perfectly spherical, changes in its motion can gravitationally interact with uneven distributions of mass in the mantle.

That interaction can slightly alter how quickly the mantle rotates, producing small changes in the length of a day.

Competing Forces Control Earth's Rotation

Another force also acts at the boundary between the core and mantle.

Known as core mantle boundary torque, it produces friction and electromagnetic drag that oppose the gravitational pull. This resistance helps limit how much Earth's day length can change.

According to the researchers, the small observed variations in the length of a day arise from subtle shifts in the balance between gravitational torque and core mantle boundary torque.

Earth's Inner Core May Be More Dynamic Than Expected

Beyond helping explain a long standing mystery about Earth's changing day length, the findings also offer new insight into what is happening deep inside the planet.

Zhang and Dumberry say the inner core appears to "deform viscously" on a time scale of about 10 years, suggesting that Earth's deepest interior may change shape and respond to forces far more dynamically than its solid composition might imply.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough explaining subtle changes in Earth's rotation by revealing dynamic interactions deep inside the planet. This discovery advances understanding of Earth's inner core and mantle behavior, which has broad scientific and educational impact.
articles.personality_title: Scientists uncover how Earth's deep core changes the length of our day
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Most people think a day is exactly 24 hours, but Earth's rotation actually changes by tiny amounts over time. These small changes affect how long a day lasts by just a few milliseconds.

**What happened** – Researchers from the University of Alberta studied how Earth's inner layers move. They found that the solid inner core, deep inside Earth, changes its spin speed. This creates a gravitational pull that affects the rocky layer above it, called the mantle. When the inner core speeds up or slows down, the mantle responds by moving the opposite way. This exchange changes Earth's rotation and the length of the day.

**Impact** – This discovery explains a mystery scientists have had for decades about why Earth's day length shifts slightly. It also shows that Earth's inner core is more active and changes shape over time, which was surprising because it is solid. Understanding these deep movements helps scientists learn more about how our planet works beneath the surface.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue studying the forces between Earth’s core and mantle to better predict changes in Earth's rotation. This could improve our knowledge of Earth's magnetic field and help with navigation systems that rely on precise time measurements.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Small shifts in Earth's deep inner core cause tiny changes in how fast the planet spins, making the length of our day vary slightly over time.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques découvrent comment le noyau profond de la Terre modifie la durée de nos journées
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La plupart des gens pensent qu'une journée dure exactement 24 heures, mais la rotation de la Terre change en réalité très légèrement avec le temps. Ces petits changements modifient la durée d'une journée de quelques millisecondes.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'Université de l'Alberta ont étudié les mouvements à l'intérieur de la Terre. Ils ont découvert que le noyau interne solide, profondément enfoui dans la Terre, change sa vitesse de rotation. Cela crée une attraction gravitationnelle qui influence la couche rocheuse au-dessus, appelée manteau. Quand le noyau interne accélère ou ralentit, le manteau réagit en bougeant dans la direction opposée. Cet échange modifie la rotation de la Terre et la durée de la journée.

**Impact** – Cette découverte explique un mystère que les scientifiques avaient depuis des décennies sur les variations de la durée du jour. Elle montre aussi que le noyau interne de la Terre est plus actif et change de forme avec le temps, ce qui est surprenant car il est solide. Comprendre ces mouvements profonds aide les scientifiques à mieux connaître le fonctionnement de notre planète.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à étudier les forces entre le noyau et le manteau pour mieux prévoir les changements dans la rotation de la Terre. Cela pourrait améliorer notre compréhension du champ magnétique terrestre et aider les systèmes de navigation qui ont besoin d'une mesure précise du temps.

**Résumé en une phrase** – De petits changements dans le noyau profond de la Terre provoquent de légères variations dans la vitesse de rotation de la planète, modifiant ainsi légèrement la durée de nos journées.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren cómo el núcleo profundo de la Tierra cambia la duración de nuestro día
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La mayoría de las personas piensa que un día dura exactamente 24 horas, pero la rotación de la Tierra en realidad cambia ligeramente con el tiempo. Estos pequeños cambios afectan la duración del día en solo unos pocos milisegundos.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Alberta estudiaron cómo se mueven las capas internas de la Tierra. Encontraron que el núcleo interno sólido, muy profundo dentro de la Tierra, cambia su velocidad de giro. Esto crea una atracción gravitatoria que afecta la capa rocosa que está encima, llamada manto. Cuando el núcleo interno acelera o desacelera, el manto responde moviéndose en la dirección opuesta. Este intercambio cambia la rotación de la Tierra y la duración del día.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento explica un misterio que los científicos tenían desde hace décadas sobre por qué la duración del día cambia ligeramente. También muestra que el núcleo interno de la Tierra es más activo y cambia de forma con el tiempo, algo sorprendente porque es sólido. Entender estos movimientos profundos ayuda a los científicos a conocer mejor cómo funciona nuestro planeta.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán estudiando las fuerzas entre el núcleo y el manto para predecir mejor los cambios en la rotación de la Tierra. Esto podría mejorar nuestro conocimiento del campo magnético terrestre y ayudar a los sistemas de navegación que dependen de mediciones precisas del tiempo.

**Frase clave** – Pequeños cambios en el núcleo profundo de la Tierra causan ligeras variaciones en la velocidad de giro del planeta, haciendo que la duración del día varíe un poco con el tiempo.
